text: When people are collaborating face to face. <break time="0.8s" /> They can easily see each other. <break time="0.8s" /> And the range of different communication cues being used. <break time="0.8s" /> So the task space is a subset of the communication space. <break time="0.8s" /> Ishii, a professor at the MIT Media Lab. <break time="0.8s" /> Describes this as seamless communication. <break time="0.8s" /> Because there is no functional separation. <break time="0.8s" /> Between the task and communication space. <break time="0.8s" /> However. <break time="0.8s" /> When people are working remotely. <break time="0.8s" /> The task space is often separated. <break time="0.8s" /> From the communication space. <break time="0.8s" /> For example. <break time="0.8s" /> When video conferencing. <break time="0.8s" /> People may have the face of their collaborator. <break time="0.8s" /> On one screen. <break time="0.8s" /> While looking at a shared document. <break time="0.8s" /> On another. <break time="0.8s" /> In this case. <break time="0.8s" /> It is impossible to see. <break time="0.8s" /> Many of the remote collaborators communication cues. <break time="0.8s" /> At the same time as looking at the task space. <break time="0.8s" /> So. <break time="0.8s" /> There is an artificial seam. <break time="0.8s" /> Between the communication space and task space. <break time="0.8s" /> This is the type of impact of remote communication technology. <break time="0.8s" /> That needs to be predicted through communication models.
